You are an expert financial-analysis assistant.  You have access to several callable tools that let you inspect a synthetic financial database constructed from Nike Inc.’s 2014 Annual Report.  Use those tools to reason step-by-step and produce a single, concrete answer to the user’s question.

Scenario (background – table values intentionally omitted):
Part II – On November 1, 2011 Nike, Inc. entered into a committed credit-facility agreement with a syndicate of banks that provides up to $1 billion of borrowings (expandable to $1.5 billion with lender approval).  After an extension on September 17, 2013, the facility now matures November 1, 2017, with a one-year extension option exercisable through October 31, 2014.  No amounts were outstanding under this facility as of May 31, 2014 or 2013.  Nike currently holds long-term debt ratings of AA- (S&P) and A1 (Moody’s).  A downgrade would increase the facility fee and interest rate; an upgrade would decrease them, but rating changes do not accelerate maturity.

Under the revolving credit facility Nike must observe several covenants, including limits on disposal of fixed assets, secured debt, and a minimum capitalization ratio.  If Nike were to violate a covenant without obtaining a waiver, any outstanding borrowings would become immediately due.  As of May 31 2014 Nike was in full compliance.

Liquidity is also provided by a $1 billion commercial-paper programme.  During fiscal-year 2014 Nike issued no commercial paper and had no outstanding balance at year-end.  Short-term debt ratings are A1+ (S&P) and P1 (Moody’s).

As of May 31 2014 Nike held $5.1 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, of which $2.5 billion was held by foreign subsidiaries.  Cash equivalents and short-term investments consist primarily of deposits at major banks, money-market funds, commercial paper, corporate notes, U.S. treasury obligations, U.S. Government-sponsored-enterprise obligations and other investment-grade fixed-income securities.  The fixed-income portfolio is exposed to credit and interest-rate risk but is entirely investment grade; average duration at year-end 2014 was 126 days.

Nike believes existing liquidity together with access to external funding is sufficient for the foreseeable future and uses tax-planning and financing strategies to manage worldwide cash.  A portion of foreign earnings is routinely repatriated (U.S. taxes already provided); a significant portion is indefinitely reinvested abroad.  If additional U.S. capital is required Nike may repatriate those funds (incurring additional U.S. tax) or issue domestic debt (incurring interest expense).

Nike also provides various indemnifications in the ordinary course of business; based on historical experience expected losses are not material.  Significant long-term contractual obligations, including endorsement contracts and lease commitments, are disclosed, covering fiscal years 2015 onward.

Tools at your disposal:
• list_commitment_types(year) → list[str]
  Return every commitment category recorded for the specified fiscal year.

• get_commitment_amount(year, commitment_type) → (amount, currency)
  Return the nominal amount and its native currency for the chosen line-item.

• get_fx_rate_for_year(year, currency) → float
  Fetch the FX rate (1 unit of currency in USD) as of 31-May of the fiscal year.

• convert_to_usd(amount, currency, year) → float
  Convert a nominal amount into USD using the year-end FX rate.

• get_commitment_amount_usd(year, commitment_type) → float
  Convenience wrapper that directly gives the USD-converted amount.

• get_average_fx_rate(year, currency) → float
  Alternate accessor for the same FX rate (may be redundant).

• get_commitments_by_currency(year, currency) → dict{commitment_type: amount}
  Retrieve all nominal amounts booked in a given currency for the year.

Question:
What percentage of the total commitments for fiscal-year 2015 were due to operating leases?

Respond with a single percentage value (e.g. “7%”) and no additional text.
